title: AeroplaneClear
question: How does an aeroplane fly?
hook: An aeroplane is not sucked up into the sky. Its wings turn the air down, and the air pushes the wing up. Tilt a wing until it stalls, pull an airliner of about 78 tonnes apart, and see why a take-off in Leh needs a longer runway.

explainer.title: The one-line idea
explainer.text: A wing makes lift by turning the air down. The air pushes the wing up, and the faster the wing moves through the air, the more it can lift.

explainer.title: The part people get wrong
explainer.text: The air over the top of a wing does not have to rush to meet the air below. That equal transit time story is wrong, and it explains only a small part of the lift.

explainer.title: Lift against drag
explainer.text: In level flight the engines push as hard as the drag pushes back. A climb needs extra thrust, and thin air at a high or hot airport means a longer take-off run.

explainer.title: Controls and flaps
explainer.text: The elevator tilts the nose, the ailerons roll, and the rudder yaws. Flaps lower the stall speed for take-off and landing, and the price is more drag.

explainer.title: The jet and the glide
explainer.text: A turbofan moves a large mass of air a little, which is efficient. With both engines stopped, the aeroplane still glides, several kilometres for each kilometre it falls.

explainer.title: How we learned
explainer.text: From Cayley's ideas and Lilienthal's gliders to the Wright brothers in 1903, Tata's first Indian licence in 1929 and the Indian Air Force in 1932.

The angle between the wing's chord line and the air flowing past it.
The point where the air separates from the top of the wing at too steep an angle, so lift falls.
The force of air resisting the aeroplane's motion, made of parasite drag and the induced drag that comes with lift.
How much lift a wing makes for each unit of drag. Airliners in cruise reach about 16 to 1.
The height in standard air that has the same density as the air you are in.
The mass of air a turbofan pushes round its core, divided by the mass that goes through the core.
The forward distance an aeroplane covers for each unit of height it loses, in still air.
